Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Put the class **alone on that line**: the line is scanned for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu to rule options out ("not a correction, feature request, or process-change") declares all of them, arming the gates those classes carry. Any explanation goes on the next line. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule. 2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes. 3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it. The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for. Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided. When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs. When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out. Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere. Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet. When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change. ` silently empties it — read the sibling, not the tag.** When a `

` is filled with raw HTML (e.g. `innerHTML`, or a framework's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `ng-bind-html`), a block element inside it (a `

`, etc.) is disallowed by the HTML content model, so the parser (browser or jsdom, same rule) auto-closes the `

` right before it and the injected content lands as the `

Skip the prose explaining what you're hoping to learn. --- # product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape, growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are **check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc (`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`). - **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true — enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"), not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to. - **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise* someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep it**. Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current. - **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source), never deleted without trace. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a ref's auto-generated name. - **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / leave. ## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

- **Default branch.** `main` stands for the repo's default branch — substitute whatever it uses.

  `conversation-logs` branch and its files, staging the `.claudinite/local/packs/` lesson onto a branch, and

  stages its lessons. Opening the lesson PR and arming its auto-merge, posting the summary, and the
  tracking-issue log go through the session's GitHub MCP tools (`mcp__github__*`) — none of those is a
  plain-git operation.
- **The repo's local packs.** Everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the canon home repo's own is
  `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/`; the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` is accepted during the rename
  window); never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.

1. **Fetch the queue.** `git fetch origin conversation-logs`; list its files
   (`git ls-tree --name-only origin/conversation-logs`). No branch, or no `*.jsonl` → stop; a quiet repo is
   the common, valid outcome.

   `config.retention_days`. Unset → the prune in step 5 is skipped entirely (capture-only adoption). (On a
   quiet repo the precondition dispatches only when retention is set *and* the branch's oldest log — by its
   filename stamp — is already past it, so a quiet dispatch always has both retention set and something to
   prune.)
3. **Fresh pass.** For each log captured in the recent window (its filename carries the capture stamp; corpus
   dedup makes an overlapping re-read harmless, so err toward re-reading the last several days): read it
   (`git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`) and run the extracting-lessons method over it — including the
   wall-time/efficiency analysis, measured from the log's own timestamps, never hand-waved.
4. **Route, land, and post.** Fold each keeper into the repo's **own local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`)
   at the local promotion ladder's strongest mechanism, exactly as
   [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) prescribes — landing the whole run through **one
   auto-merging PR** (title `Claudinite growth: conversation extract`, its commit referencing the worked issue
   so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes), armed for auto-merge the same way
   [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) delivers: GitHub squash-merges it once the repo's checks pass,
   with no human review. For each rule that actually landed, post **one short comment** via
   `add_issue_comment` on the issue named in the log's filename (`--issue-<n>--`) — where **`--issue-0--`
   means the capture had no associated issue** (a session-end capture), so there is nothing to post on and
   the rule simply lands without a comment: one provenance line (the
   rule added, the capture date, the session id), then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of
   conversation that caused the rule — what was asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule
   follows from it. Summarize, never transcribe: the dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue, so no
   pasted turns beyond a short quoted phrase, and never the log. A log that yields nothing gets **no**

   `retention_days` days, give it a **final hindsight pass** — one last read against the now-current corpus
   (steps 3–4 apply to anything it still yields) — then `git rm` it on the `conversation-logs` branch and push

The standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Conversation Extract`** in this repo —
found by that exact title, never a number; created **closed** if missing; its state never changed afterward.
When a run lands a lesson, posts a summary, or prunes logs, log it as one dated comment (via
`add_issue_comment`) naming what changed; a run that changed nothing logs nothing.

Whether a lesson clears the bar — and whether the hindsight pass should overturn a fresh-pass call — is the

`agent_model: opus`; the executor dispatches its subagent there.

- **Never paste the conversation onto an issue** — not raw JSONL, not a rendered transcript, not the turns

1	# Conversation extract — the growth pack's conversation-side daily task
2	
3	The conversation-side sibling of [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md): mine this repo's captured
4	conversation logs for durable lessons, post a short summary of the exchange behind each extracted rule on the
5	issue it was worked under, and prune logs past retention. You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue. The
6	access model matches growth-extract — the repo's own content is plain **local git** in the checkout; only the
7	GitHub **issue/PR API** goes through MCP. (Capture, which needs the live session transcript, is the separate
8	in-session step at merge; this task consumes what capture already pushed.)
9	
10	The **method** — the friction signals, the measured efficiency analysis, the lesson bar — stays canonical in
11	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) and is not restated here. The captured log carries what
12	that method needs: per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the tool_use/tool_result pairs behind
13	wall-time numbers.
14	
15	## Conventions used in this doc
16	
17	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for the repo's default branch — substitute whatever it uses.
18	- **Access split — local git for repo content, MCP for PRs and the issue API.** Reading the
19	  `conversation-logs` branch and its files, staging the `.claudinite/local/packs/` lesson onto a branch, and
20	  the retention prune are all **plain git in this repo's checkout** (`git fetch`/`show`/`rm`/`push`) — the
21	  branch is *in this repo*, so no cross-repo access is involved, exactly as growth-extract reads `git log` and
22	  stages its lessons. Opening the lesson PR and arming its auto-merge, posting the summary, and the
23	  tracking-issue log go through the session's GitHub MCP tools (`mcp__github__*`) — none of those is a
24	  plain-git operation.
25	- **The repo's local packs.** Everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the canon home repo's own is
26	  `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/`; the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` is accepted during the rename
27	  window); never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
28	
29	## The run
30	
31	1. **Fetch the queue.** `git fetch origin conversation-logs`; list its files
32	   (`git ls-tree --name-only origin/conversation-logs`). No branch, or no `*.jsonl` → stop; a quiet repo is
33	   the common, valid outcome.
34	2. **Read retention.** From this repo's `.claudinite-checks.json`, the grow_with_claudinite entry's
35	   `config.retention_days`. Unset → the prune in step 5 is skipped entirely (capture-only adoption). (On a
36	   quiet repo the precondition dispatches only when retention is set *and* the branch's oldest log — by its
37	   filename stamp — is already past it, so a quiet dispatch always has both retention set and something to
38	   prune.)
39	3. **Fresh pass.** For each log captured in the recent window (its filename carries the capture stamp; corpus
40	   dedup makes an overlapping re-read harmless, so err toward re-reading the last several days): read it
41	   (`git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`) and run the extracting-lessons method over it — including the
42	   wall-time/efficiency analysis, measured from the log's own timestamps, never hand-waved.
43	4. **Route, land, and post.** Fold each keeper into the repo's **own local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`)
44	   at the local promotion ladder's strongest mechanism, exactly as
45	   [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) prescribes — landing the whole run through **one
46	   auto-merging PR** (title `Claudinite growth: conversation extract`, its commit referencing the worked issue
47	   so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes), armed for auto-merge the same way
48	   [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) delivers: GitHub squash-merges it once the repo's checks pass,
49	   with no human review. For each rule that actually landed, post **one short comment** via
50	   `add_issue_comment` on the issue named in the log's filename (`--issue-<n>--`) — where **`--issue-0--`
51	   means the capture had no associated issue** (a session-end capture), so there is nothing to post on and
52	   the rule simply lands without a comment: one provenance line (the
53	   rule added, the capture date, the session id), then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of
54	   conversation that caused the rule — what was asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule
55	   follows from it. Summarize, never transcribe: the dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue, so no
56	   pasted turns beyond a short quoted phrase, and never the log. A log that yields nothing gets **no**
57	   comment — extraction is the only path to permanence. Finding nothing at all is fine and common.
58	5. **Retention prune.** When `retention_days` is set: for each log whose filename stamp is older than
59	   `retention_days` days, give it a **final hindsight pass** — one last read against the now-current corpus
60	   (steps 3–4 apply to anything it still yields) — then `git rm` it on the `conversation-logs` branch and push
61	   (commit message ending `[skip ci]`). The branch is never merged and its history is never rewritten — plain
62	   add/remove commits only. This push to the non-default logs branch is outside the outcome taxonomy (DESIGN §1).
63	
64	## Tracking: log each run under the task's own issue
65	
66	The standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Conversation Extract`** in this repo —
67	found by that exact title, never a number; created **closed** if missing; its state never changed afterward.
68	When a run lands a lesson, posts a summary, or prunes logs, log it as one dated comment (via
69	`add_issue_comment`) naming what changed; a run that changed nothing logs nothing.
70	
71	## Run on a capable model
72	
73	Whether a lesson clears the bar — and whether the hindsight pass should overturn a fresh-pass call — is the
74	judgment this task exists for, and its PR auto-merges without a human review gate. This task declares
75	`agent_model: opus`; the executor dispatches its subagent there.
76	
77	## What this task must never do
78	
79	- **Never merge `conversation-logs`** anywhere, and never rewrite its history — plain add and remove commits
80	  only.
81	- **Never paste the conversation onto an issue** — not raw JSONL, not a rendered transcript, not the turns
82	  themselves. Each landed rule gets one ≤200-word summary of the exchange behind it, and nothing more.
83	- **Never delete a log younger than retention, and never delete anything while `retention_days` is unset** —
84	  deletion is the ack that both passes happened.
85	- **Never touch the shared canon** — writes go to the repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/` (via an
86	  auto-merging PR), its issues, and its logs branch; lifting portable lessons is the central promote task's job.

1	# Extracting lessons from a working session
2	
3	> **Scope: a single agent ↔ user conversation.** This doc is the **method** for mining one
4	> working session's *dialogue and the actions taken in it* for improvements. It is **not** the
5	> growth extract ([the growth-extract task](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) that mines **issues, PRs, and commits** over repo
6	> history — that routine never sees a conversation. Its two callers: the
7	> [conversation-extract daily task](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md), which applies it to **captured**
8	> conversation logs — where the friction signals below (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a
9	> wait you sat through) survive with their timestamps — and an owner's occasional plain-words
10	> ask for a retrospective over the live session.
11	
12	Portable guidance for mining an agent ↔ user session — a Claude Code web session, a CLI run, a
13	captured conversation log — for durable improvements: read the conversation and convert its
14	friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less dependent on human
15	feedback.
16	
17	Run the reflection on a **capable model.** Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears
18	the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong
19	"lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
20	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model
21	to the judgment it must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the
22	separate efficiency analysis — also live there; this doc is the how-to.
23	
24	## The goal
25	
26	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less
27	rework, less waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but
28	as "where did this cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost
29	next time." If a pass can't name a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's
30	fine (see [No new lessons](#no-new-lessons-is-a-valid--and-common--result)).
31	
32	## When it runs
33	
34	Routinely, in the [conversation-extract daily task](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md) over each captured
35	log (a fresh pass within a day of capture, a final hindsight pass before retention deletes the
36	log) — the standard path. If an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective over the live
37	session, apply the same method and deliver the capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**,
38	never one that self-merges (the nightly auto-merges its own PR per its own doc; a live retrospective
39	wants human eyes). **Never
40	reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner
41	decides when a session is done enough to mine.
42	
43	## What to look for — the friction signals
44	
45	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop
46	cost more than necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
47	
48	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
49	
50	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I
51	meant…"); the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same
52	request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
53	
54	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every
55	question the user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate
56	**convention or glossary entry**; a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first
57	checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc the agent reads cold and gets right the first
58	time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds correctly **without the round-trip**.
59	
60	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
61	
62	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran
63	a command that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light
64	one fit; reinvented something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written
65	to "verify"; missed an existing convention and had it corrected in review.
66	
67	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing
68	helper/convention so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read.** Place
69	it by where the trap is hit, not in a central bucket: a gotcha from **misusing a specific API,
70	class, or library goes as a comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where
71	the next editor of that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list.
72	Co-locate it in a file's own header comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only
73	hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a central gotchas doc for what no single usage site
74	owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant file (a mistake of omission), or a
75	cross-cutting invariant. The test: next time the agent takes the good path first, not after a
76	detour.
77	
78	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
79	
80	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been
81	parallel; a padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its
82	result was already in hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already
83	green.
84	
85	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers and separate the
86	kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting** (sleeps,
87	polling, a finished process not yet killed). A captured log carries per-entry timestamps and
88	per-message token usage, so the numbers are computable, not estimated. A fix is only credible
89	against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
90	was already optimal.
91	
92	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
93	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the
94	subject of the standing **efficiency analysis** in
95	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold a wall-time
96	finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
97	loss of quality.
98	
99	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
100	
101	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks
102	*repeatedly* are a checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how
103	many processes ran — could it be fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its
104	work was done?", stop waiting to be asked — fold those exact questions into a **standing
105	self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the relevant work, and close with a
106	terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each recurring question
107	converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
108	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively,
109	with numbers.
110	
111	## From signal to lesson — the bar
112	
113	A friction signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and
114	generalizable beyond this one session.** Before adding anything:
115	
116	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded
117	  differently, even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
118	- **Route to the local pack that owns it, and prefer the strongest mechanism** — the **local
119	  promotion ladder**, at the project's own level. A project's capture surface is its **local
120	  packs** (`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/`): pick the pack whose territory the lesson belongs
121	  to, then a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in that pack's `rules` (its failure message
122	  *is* the lesson; ship it with a red-first fixture), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a
123	  **pack skill**, and only what neither can carry lands as terse **prose** in the pack's
124	  `RULES.md`. Write more checks and less prose — a check relieves every session's context
125	  completely where prose only relocates it. A gotcha tied to one call site still goes as a
126	  comment at that site (above), not into any pack. When no pack's scope fits and the lesson
127	  warrants segregation, a new local pack is a self-contained directory drop.
128	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared,
129	  cross-project canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote
130	  stage lifts it there centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever
131	  travels.
132	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or
133	  something already implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
134	
135	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
136	
137	Most sessions yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write nothing
138	rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes
139	the canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a
140	genuinely new, reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

`maintenance.delivery` is `auto-merge`, but this repo's `.github/workflows/ci.yml` declares only `pull_request` and `push`. - Canon: teach `bootstrap.md` Part 8 to ship the trigger (and say why), and make `conformance-workflow` flag an unfiltered-but-undispatchable sweep — the same dead end the path-filter case already covers.
